p: That’s the Tony Albarado way, like how he used to do. Go ahead.
Yeah, so the Teaching Fellows Program -
Those have been around for a long time. Go ahead.
Teaching Fellows Program does directly that, attract people who have maybe a major -
No, I know, I know.
We also have a Teach Where You Belong Campaign that launched on social media.
Okay, so you’ll give us at some point how many have been recruited next year, right specifically Art Teachers?
Yup.

So, the - my understanding is that students in the 8th grade are

not necessarily meeting their requirements in terms of arts education. So, how many schools do not have a full time or part time certified arts teacher? What are you doing about it? Where are students not meeting the state mandated level of arts instruction? How will you or will you update the Blue Print, which I love that was some time ago. And then, how many, what’s the percentage or number of students enrolled in Arts Education. I’m a huge supporter of Arts Education.
Yes, uh, Gale and I know that well.
Yes, you do.

We’ve hosted many programs as with CBOs at Lincoln Center and so on. So, thank you for your constant support in this area. I’m going to turn it over to Deputy Chancellor, First Deputy Chancellor to talk a little bit more about our arts work.

Good morning. Danielle Giunta, so in passionate agreement with you. Every child in New York City Public Schools deserves equitable access to an incredible arts offering. Uhm, to some of your questions, we have 99 percent of all of our

students are receiving arts instruction and support. Some through certified arts teachers and some through uh great organization partnerships as you know and our cultural organizations grant funded initiatives and then district provided arts programming. For recruitment, we received about 391 applications from teachers in the arts uhm last year. I don’t know if Ms. Way has an updated number but we’re keeping an eye on that as well.
Okay, because my information here is 31 percent of 8th graders don’t meet the learning requirement and then what about the Blue Print?

So, with regards to that, so you know 8.4 percent of schools serving 7-12 right do not have a certified art teacher and that’s uhm part of what we’re talking about in terms of you know using CBOs and so on to really try to uhm fill that gap and the Blue Print conversation I think we can get back to you on that. I’m not sure -

Okay, I want just quickly one more thing, if I could ask because the Chancellor talked a lot so I lost some time.

So, I want to know about GNT because you didn’t mention it. I love GNT, not everybody does and secondly, how many more 1972 Broadways are there and how much rent are they paying and are they vacant?

Alright, so I’m about to turn over or that conversation to uhm, the conversation about 1972 Broadway just to give some context. There are some buildings which included 1972 Broadway at one point that were Pre-K buildings that were empty and Gale and I when I was a superintendent worked to make sure that that building is now occupied. The conversation on GNT is something that’s very important to many of our families across the city. I am super committed to making sure that our families have access to accelerated opportunities in schools. We’ll be launching soon enough in the upcoming weeks and months an engagement conversation specifically regarding GNT starting with schools like the Anderson School and others around the city.
I would like to be part of that conversation.
Yes, you will be Gale, I promise.
What about my 1972’s?
Yup.
Council Member looked directly at me for that answer.
Yes, I did.
Uhm, we have 20-
And Lincoln. Lincoln has a 1972 also.

THere are 27 - 1972’s and for folks who may not know what that means, they are city owned or leased buildings that are currently unoccupied. 1060 Flatbush was once - 1070, 1070, thank you. Thank you was once 1972 and it now has an AIMs program.
Okay.
And so as you know Council Member, that number was once 40. It is now down to 27 and so, we are getting that number down as we continue to get additional resources and investment.
Okay but those are all paying rent, I assume.
Not all. Some of them are owned by the city.
Okay, can you get us an amount that is dollar rent is being paid?
So, we have to confirm that with SCA. We do have some limitations in sharing lease costs in terms because it can impede negotiations with the landlords but we will confirm that.
Alright, thank you.
Thank you Council Member Brewer. Council Member Narcisse.

Uhm, thank you Mr. Chair for the opportunity and I want to say congratulations again Mr. Chancellor and Deputy Chancellor as we’re talking about enrollment, slot configuration, I hope that my zip code, some of the zip code that I have is in need for that - dying need. So, many questions that I have but I’m going to keep it tight for you and try to answer it as much because the time is not on my side. The state's new temperature law which took effect September 2025 now prohibits occupancy above 88 fahrenheit and requires that mitigation at 82 degrees fahrenheit. Uh, DOE is therefore out of compliance in their own building. How many schools currently have no safe alternative space for students when common areas are over heated in that specific capital investments

plans are there to finally bring the gyms cafeterias and the clinics into compliance?

Yeah, thank you for that question. We have over the last number of years, had significant investment in a seize through our schools and uhm, and also through the help of so many of you on the Council. Uhm, significant investment in Reso A grants for common areas but if uh Kevin, I don’t know if you want to add anything else.

Yes, very much plan to be in compliance with the state law here. Our schools are equipped uh, our custodians are equipped with several mechanisms to measure indoor room temperatures. I would say we benefitted greatly from the AC For All initiative. That ensured air conditioning and electricity was brought to each and every single classroom, over 69,000 classrooms -

Thank you for the classroom. I’m specifically talking about the common areas, cafeterias, gym, because I have many of them in my district right now and will not go in the summer time. They are heated badly.
Yeah and in part -
They need to be fixed.
And in part why I was bringing up the classrooms is because there’s some 69,000 classrooms where -
I appreciate it.

Where we would bring kids for breakfast or lunch, if we had to in egregious heat wave or we could do move to improve and do exercise within said classrooms. So, part of our contingency plan is like, if you cannot use the said gymnasium or said, can you use the classroom. So, we do have classrooms and other spaces. We’re well over 50 percent in compliance with public assemblies. We do require infrastructure development and making capital investments in those classrooms and gymnasiums. And I thank -

I appreciate it. Let’s say specifics because I have a few questions. You cannot play basketball in the classroom. Uhm, you can not have a play in the classroom. Uhm, giving the federal uncertainty around uhm Title 1 and other education funding streams. What happens to schools that rely on federal dollars to purchase textbooks and classroom supplies if those funds are cut or frozen?

Yeah, thank you for - thank you for the question. I think you know all of us are concerned with uhm our schools and their funding and that’s why it’s great that the vast majority of the funds that comes to NYC Public Schools actually end up directly in our schools and specifically in thinking about what we - what, what happens in terms of Title 1 and Seritta, do you want to add anything there?

Yeah, so just wanted to add like we’re very well aware of all of the uncertainty that’s happening at the federal level. And so, any reduction in our federal funding would be disastrous, especially since it actually supports some of our most vulnerable students. I think it would definitely initiate conversations with both our local and state partners to ensure that we are maintaining those critical resources to our schools.

For the paraprofessional, we talking about recruitment and retention? You can recruit but if you’re not paying, you cannot retain. Uhm, now we have so many classes, so many classrooms that need support and they, according to the teachers, they’re not getting the

support. Paraprofessionals - we know they are very essential with uhm, IEPs, receiving their mandated services. What is the current vacancy rate for the paraprofessionals citywide? I think you said about 1,300, 13- something. So, what - compared to last - I mean year before, how many was it? Because now I think it’s 13, 1,300 something.

Speaking to that issue a little bit, we have to also acknowledge like our like my cabinet pointed out earlier, there’s a structural uh impediment that creates even a greater need for paraprofessionals and so, we applaud and we appreciate your desire to push for increased pay at the Council. We thank you for that but in terms of specific uh specially what it was last year, I’m not sure we have that but we can easily get that to you.
Okay, thank you. How many schools, if any, currently lack a full time dedicated school nurse?
Uhm, yeah, Kevin, do you have thoughts on that.
Every school has access and any student has access to health services for any student enrolled at the school.

Okay, I appreciate it. Uhm, for the EI- I mean, IEP, thank you so much for this young lady that kind of put it out for me. I always wonder about EIP program and you give it to me. Uhm, the cap we’re talking about. I am so not with it because we’re spending a lot of money while New York City actually our DOE can get the job done without going to a private. What are we doing actually to reach the level that we can be advocate with you and encourage back to make sure the children are in DOE and we’re not being pennywise dollar foolish?
Uhm, well, first of all, thank you for calling me young lady.
I don’t know your name. You are young.
Liz Vladeck, thank you. Uhm-
You’re young.

So, as the least informed person at this table about pedagogy in particular, I think the real partnership we need is to understand the quality of programming is to understand what it actually takes for a student with disabilities to succeed. You know I think DC Foti could not be more clear how

well she and her teams understand that and the distinction that I’ve been drawing is that we don’t see that same kind of information, transparency, uhm, you know grades, test results, when for all of the money that’s going outside of our system. So, I -that’s where we really need some help is to see more public interest in what’s actually happening with all those dollars that are going out the door. Because remember, while I - you know while we have a total of this year, I think we’ll in somewhere around 16,000 cases. Each case is assessed individually by a hearing officer who isn’t concerned about what’s going on at that particular school or what could we be doing. They don’t see the bigger picture. So, we need help with that bigger picture assessment and setting public expectations for what our dollars should pay for.

Yeah, because I have a case right now in my office they’re coming back and forth and it’s a simple thing. The recommendation was done by the therapist, by everyone that assessed the child for - to have a phone, to use the phone because that eased her up in the classroom and we did not do that and that probably costing you over

probably you say $144,000. I don’t know. So, now we’re going to have to do better with that. So, I see my Chair giving me a hand even though I’m excited whenever I’m in front of DOE. So, thank you so much for all your work. I appreciate you.

If I may Council Member, we would love to follow up. We use those when people raise up, oh, I have a particular case, we really like to get in and see what’s going on so we know, oh did something just go wrong here or is there actually something that we need to fix. If you wouldn’t mind reaching out, we would like to follow up.
I’m ready to work with you. I love my children in New York City.
Great.
Thank you.

Thank you Council Member Narcisse. It seems very clear we on this Committee care a lot about our kids with disabilities, kids with IEPs, we are also interested in making sure we have the investments, to make sure that our public system can and does provide the services to our kids who need them and I think we’re all in agreement there and we’d like to see the investments made.

Turning it over to Council Member Wong.

Thank you Chair. Thank you Chancellor and members of the panel for coming today. Uhm, uhm, before I get to my uh district questions, I just want to uh talk about my experience in attending PEP meetings. Because I serve them on the school board, PEP 24 and after that I serve as budget director of the former Councilman Robert Holden. I attend a lot of PEP meetings and quite often they talk about contracts. They vote on contracts but one thing I noticed that there’s no mentioning of how many students it impacts. We have contracts that may impact a few hundred and then there are contracts 1,000 and there may be contracts that affect 100,000. Is this something you want to consider including that in voting on contracts because if I don’t know and I’m sure to the parents, a lot of them will be clueless but they’re very concerned about these issues. Can you address that?

Yeah, thank you so much for the question and I think you know when we’re thinking about what the PEP wants to look at and when we’re thinking about contracts, people do want to know what

the impact is and I think that’s something we can look into and take back and consider.

Okay thank you, yes. Okay, I’m going to move forward to my district questions. Uh, my district, District 30 includes some of the most engaged public school families in Queens, families in Elmhurst, Masbeth, Middle Village, Richwood, Glendale and Rico Park. Families who also rely on parochial and non-public schools that are now facing closures and added pressure. I also represent PS IS 128. When the school community has serious concerns about a proposed lithium ion battery facility being built directly across from the school. In a situation like this, the Department cannot sit on the sidelines. We need to know where DOE stands and what it is doing to protect that school community. At the same time, we’re heading into an FY27 budget with real fiscal pressure. If we are asking schools and families to do more with less, we need to start by looking inward. We cannot keep expanding central bureaucracy while classroom feels the squeeze.

So, my first question is, uhm PS IS 128, has DOE conducted any safety assessments for PS IS 128 given the proposed facility that’s across the street and is right next to the annex of the school?

Yeah, thank you and you know whenever things arise close to our schools, they are certainly of concern to us and so, I’m going to turn it over to Kevin Moran to see if there is anything that we’ve thought of there.

Yes, thank you for the question and understand your concerns regarding battery storage. This is an evolving technology and evolving infrastructure in the City of New York and its heavily regulated. We would defer to our partners at the Department of Buildings and Department of Health for a follow up here. Certainly want to learn more about that actual location but I have seen, as many New Yorkers have seen these uh so far as being close to gas stations and then causing concern. So, I want to learn a little bit more about this specific issue and then come back to you.
Okay, what is DOEs position on this facility? Do you have one?
We’re not the regulator of the facility but we’re going to follow up with our interagency partners to come back to you.

Okay, thank you. Uhm, next, last week in IS 93, there was a carbon monoxide incident in which I got updates from Speaker Julie Menin’s Office and from the FDNY and from the Superintendents office but there seems to be a conflict of stories where one message says students were evacuated, another said the students were in the cafeteria. When did DOE first become aware of the issue and was there a full evacuation?

Yeah, each school has a building response team and the principal is a part of that. We notify first responders of any incident like this. FDNY does come to the building and recommends evacuation or not. They also give us the all clear. In that specific case, students were relocated and students were allowed back in the building after it was given the all clear. If you want a timeline of the notification from the superintendent and the FDNY, I can provide that to you.
Yes, please do.
Absolutely.
And usually the BRT, the Building Response Team is, they have a note taker that actually should outline a time.

Okay thank you. Parents call our office first when they heard about it and then we gave them conflicting answers and we couldn’t explain the inconsistencies. Thank you. Uhm, the next, uhm, I talk to principals and I hear from them consistently that in my district that decisions are still being driven from Tweed and not from the school level. Do you agree that DOE is still operating as a top down system Chancellor?

Well, first of all, thank you for that question and there are times - one of the things that I think is a challenge for any Chancellor and certainly something I’m thinking about is at what point- points are we a system of schools? That means individual schools have the autonomy to be able to do the things that they see fit and at what points are we a school system. That means that there ought to be some uh, citywide things that we believe uhm, are baselined that we need at every single school. And so, uh one example, is New York City Reads, where

we’re saying look, we need and we believe that all of our young people should have access to grade level content and we should be clear about the interventions that we’re doing when our young people are off track. And so, that - I make no apologies for that. I think that should be a citywide conversation and there will be other times when certainly schools can at their own uhm, topic or their own flavor if you will. Each district has its own flavor, each school has its own unique concerns but there are times and we want those times to be when they are high leverage times. So, when we’re talking about what’s our city’s response to students with disabilities. What’s our city’s response to multilingual learners? Those things are find to be things that we stand on because we believe that they are that important. But then there are other things that certainly schools can have an individual response to.
Okay, thank you Chancellor.
Thank you Council Member Wong. We’re going to - yes, I’ll put you down for the next round. Council Member Won.
Thank you so much. It’s a little confusing right, Wong and Won?
No, it’s fine. It’s fine.

It’s good to see you all. Thank you so much to Chair Dinowitz. I want to go into my district numbers for the 2025 to 2029 Capital Plan. So, according to your report right now for District 30, there is 1,146 new total funded sites in progress. Can you help me understand which schools this is referring to? Because for the 1LIC project and for previous landuse development in Long Island City, we have had outstanding investments and I know that right now in the Executive Budget, my district is missing the Department of Education funding for $152 million outstanding for 5-46 46th Avenue, the middle school. That is long overdue. And then $367 million outstanding for two elementary schools that are badly needed because of the amount of development that the district has taken in with the amount of waitlists for my children. As well as understanding how we have to adhere to the fair classes sizes rule. So, can you help me understand one, why is the $152 million plus $367 million missing in the Executive Budget, though promised by the Admin as

well as supported by the current Mayor, who represented this district prior to becoming Mayor? And what the current budget is for District 30 that you’re accounting for?
Yeah.
So, trying to understand the difference.
Okay, uhm, I think Kevin or Erin, you have thoughts?

My preference on this question in particular is to hold it to the SCA Capital hearing. They have the latest figures. We actually just met with them on this very topic on Wednesday. So, I prefer the SCA President applying here.

Okay because I do speak closely with the President and her Chief of Staff and I want to make sure that the written promises are kept for my district because for the last ten years, for all the schools that were promised. They were all delayed because we did not have proper funding. Another question that I have is - well, I’ll ask during the SCA hearing as well but the BSGE Highschool so Bachelorette School of Global Education is fully funded. So, I just want to make sure that

that’s confirmed on record. And I also want to understand, what is the plan going forward to also think about right sizing our schools or creating space for existing buildings. For example, PS 111 in my district services mostly Queens Bridge Houses and Ravenswoods Houses residents. Yet, they have been fighting back on the colocation of vocal char- uh voice charter school and they’ve been asking for the school to be no longer colocated. So, as we try to adhere to the fair classes rule, how are we also looking at spaces that are being forced to colocate with Charter Schools to make space to adhere to this mandate?

Yeah, that’s a great question. And so, something that we’ve over the last uh, number of weeks and something that as I came into this role, was really deeply thinking about, which is how do we make fully use of our existing spaces. And so, we’ve had significant conversations with our SCA partners around this and uhm, we’re developing a citywide utilization strategy that’s actually going to address exactly what you’re talking about, specifically for District 30. I don’t know if you had anything to add there Erin?
Well, your specific question around colocation.
Yup, of Charter Schools being removed from Public Schools.

That’s right, so currently we follow the law, the Charter law, which requires us to offer space or pay rental assistance. So, I understand your question. There’s no intention right now to remove colocated schools as a policy matter but there may be school utilization proposals in the future that do contemplate that. Also, there could be vendors themselves or Charters themselves that look for rental assistance; something we would support.

So, I want to make sure that it’s on record that PS 111 should be a standalone school to make sure that our children, especially of the lowest income are being counted for and if we’re going to adhere to fair classes rule, that means that we have to remove Voice Charter School from that school so that we don’t have to build a whole new standalone building but we should just relocate the Charter and pay for their rent elsewhere. If you can keep an eye on that.
Noted.

We’ve - we’ve also for the last four years, have invested over $100 million for our school upgrades for buildings that are over 100 years old that continue to be- remain unspent. Can you help me understand why there is such a delay in capital funding being spent to maintain our schools for simple things like sensory gyms or wall dividers for the auditorium/gym natatorium so that kids can play freely? What is the hold up? Because year to year, I continue to be told by SCA that we just have to wait and there’s no clarity on why. For four years it hasn’t moved.

I could do this at the Capital Hearing or if it's - I could do it now, if it’s helpful. Uhm - wait? Do it now? Okay, so that’s an excellent question. Uh, at the heart of the matter was a broken system in our capital reimbursement program. That essentially took all the Reso A grants uhm and introduced a we’ll pay for it with tax levy first, reimburse at the end of the year later with capital dollars. What happened in that process was largely disallowances and problems with us losing money year

over year. That process has since changed. I testified last year, we had 700 some jobs in the backlog and roughly $50 million going into our new capital reimbursement system. We recently just crossed the $210 million capital threshold system. In that, we have no disallowances, we have dollar for dollar project going out the door. There are currently - this is - I was saving this for the Capital hearing. About 73 jobs left in our backlog. Uhm and so what we’re doing now I could provide to you for the first time ever, a full list of where every project is that you funded and whether it’s in scope, design, award, or what phase in construction and it will be member specific. So, I could send that to each member and it goes back. So, you’ll have a full allocation. I’ll tell you this time next year, we will not have a backlog. It will be project for project. We’ll make sure those critical investments happen.
Thank you so much. Thank you Council Member Won. We’re going to go on to round two. Council Member Banks.

Thank you and I would be remiss again Chancellor for not thanking you and your

team for coming to Thomas Jefferson High School. We appreciate that. Back to the young adult borough centers. I just want to relay some of the concerns that was expressed to me by parents and uhm, and some of the students. Uh, the unsafe - they said it is unsafe for students who are overage and undercredited trying to finish high school hours for the YABC from 4:00 p.m. to 10 p.m. to now have to travel far out of Brownsville, East New York to Bensonhurst and Coney Island. They said South Shore has a gang problem. That some of these students have gang issues. Medgar Evers School and Thomas Jefferson creates a safe corridor, right on Pennsylvania for these students. And you know I just want to - again, I just want to reiterate their needs - there should have been an impact study done or conversation earlier on before we were removed from the RFP. To me- uh this to me makes no sense, that a district that has historically been left behind, now to add insult to injury and to continue to hurt these students by having them have to travel close to two hours into Bensonhurst and to Coney Island.

Uhm, I don’t want to belabor that anymore but I’m hoping that you seriously reconsider that and you stop this injustice from taking place to our students in the 42nd Council District. Now, turning to pupil transportation and uh, safety, student safety. Over the past two years, my office has received multiple complaints from parents about the serious transportation failures. Students being left on buses, routes changing without notice, and overcrowded buses, where children including those IEPs do not have proper seating and/or accommodations. And in each of these cases, the students required additional support. What is DOE doing to address these failures, particularly for students who rely on these services the most?

Uh, well two things. I will be looking into the issue you raised before. I was a Deputy Superintendent in Brownsville. I recognize that you know, Brownsville to Coney Island is far. And so that - that -
And East New York.

Yeah, right, exactly and so that’s - I can see that difficulty and so, we’ll look into that issue.

Uhm, when it comes to pupil transportation, that’s something that you know as a former principal, superintendent in two districts, that was - that was one of the things that was constant no matter where I worked in the city. There was significant concern with pupil transportation and I think over the last year, year or so and certainly recently we’ve been working on some modernization efforts that I think have uhm, you know contributed positively to some of this work. So, I’m going to turn it over to Kevin Moran to talk a little bit more about that.

Yeah, this is so vital for our students that rely on yellow school bus transportation. For the nine out of ten kids that do not get a yellow school bus, we also want to provide them opportunities like ferry discounts, OMNY cards four trips a day, 365. I also want to see how far we could expand that to the one in ten kids who rely on yellow school bus. And the goal with yellow school bus service is to improve each and every day. One of the things we did foundationally and this was basically at the prodding of the City Council Local Law 32, 33, and 34, was introduce a modernization effort. One that parents can track and

find data where they needed to be and actually hold people accountable. The first thing was a New York City School Bus App, so I encourage everyone to go to NYXA, download that app. Now we’ll be able to time what time they get on and what time they get off and the routes will be much more efficient going forward. But we do want to have other places for parents to file complaints. So, we’re going to try to have the app do that.
Right.

We’ll actually roll up all that in aggregate on the website so parents could see how each vendor is doing. We could then use corrective action to hold vendors accountable. Something quite frankly we haven’t done a good job at.

And that’s - that’s what I want to hone in on - on the accountability because there are parents that have the app but they are finding their child to be left in the bus lot where the child should be home. I have had multiple situations and we’ve advocated for parents, who the child has been left on the bus. Uhm, or have been dropped off at a location that they shouldn’t be dropped off at and then nowadays, uh that just -

that, that, that just to me for most parents, that’s something obviously that is unacceptable. So, uhm if we can, you know see more reforms done there, so we can put our students safety first. Thank you.
Absolutely. Thank you Chair.
Thank you Council Member Banks. Council Member Hanks.

Hanks, Banks. Thank you so much Chair. Uhm, I just have a few questions. In your testimony Chancellor, I was excited to hear the Administration will be building on this Council’s investment and creating culturally responsive resources for Black, Latino and Hidden Voices curriculum. I find that to be fantastic. You said that you would be launching a comprehensive professional learning plan to expand the use of materials in classrooms across the city. So, I just wanted to understand a little bit more like what is that plan to ensure that all schools across the city are going to be equitable in getting that information. How are they going to get informed and how are we going to make sure that the resources are implemented

seamlessly and impactful implemented. So, I want to know how that magic is going to happen.

Alright, thank you so much for lifting this. Uh, it’s something that’s really passionate, I’m really passionate about. We, uh, as a superintendent, I implemented the Black studies curriculum and started that curriculum in my district and I you know there’s one thing though to make the curriculum available to everyone and resources available to everyone. It’s a different, it’s a different thing to say, let’s make sure our teachers with everything that they have going on understand how to seamlessly weave what the work is into their lesson plan or else it won’t be - it won’t be used as efficiently. And so, we’ve seen significant interest in this from teachers. There is uhm, uhm, a huge number of downloads of the Black studies curriculum in particular. A lot of resources and hidden voices. And so, we have a three different layers providing professional learning. There will be professional learning provided by uhm, the New York City Social Studies Department. There will be work that we’re going to be doing with partners such as facing

history and others and then there’s also work that’s already being provi- uh done - uh this is the work from the City Council’s work with work as well as the ECO foundation and so, you know I’m going to turn it over to our deputy chancellor, First Deputy Chancellor to talk a little bit more about process and getting - making sure that we try to get this as much as possible in the classrooms.

Thank you and thank you so much for your excitement. Uhm, when I was a superintendent, uh one of my schools had a student equity team that presented me with a letter about making sure our libraries had books that were Windows and Mirrors. I’m sure you’ve heard that frame before. Uhm, and so, I’ve been just so excited that the agency has built out the Hidden Voices curriculum. That your support has allowed us to bring in the Black studies and Latina curriculum and also that we’ve built Tech Sets that are available digitally through our library to make sure that these culturally responsive books are in the hands of our students and their families to really get at that CRSC.

So, now that we have HQIM through the High Quality Instructional Materials in our schools and we have these resources, we want to have a more intentional approach on how we support our teachers and aligning those curriculum, not replacing HQIM but really lifting up any gaps or making the CRSC approach more rich. So, we’re going to be thinking about this in different phases, piloting some districts. We already have the Black City’s curriculum started in two pilot districts. It expanded across 18. There are 32,000 downloads of the curriculum. We have momentum over access and use but what we need to your point, to Chancellor’s point is that strategic coordinated uhm approach. And so some steps that we’re taking is also thinking about how we do crosswalks where we show our teachers in this unit whether it’s your ELA unit and we’re preparing for all three curricular choices across the city or within passport. Uhm, where you can use these units and these resources integrated seamlessly. We’ll start this in some small scale. We have a long term plan to scale up from there and then make sure that we’re touching every one of our schools.

Thank you so much. I have one more question before my time runs out. Uhm, so families in Staten Island often lack uhm access to 3K seats forcing long commutes. We also did not get any 2K seats as part of the Administrations roll out. And is there a reason why you know that this roll out happened the way it did and is there an opportunity to add 12 to 15 K seats in Staten Island if we have a provider to do so? We can talk offline.
